title: About Vaccine Information Statements
text: A Vaccine Information Statement, or VIS, is a CDC document explaining the benefits and risks of a vaccine. It helps patients, parents, and legal representatives understand information about vaccination. U.S. vaccine providers must give the relevant current VIS before each dose of vaccines covered by the federal Vaccine Injury Act. This applies to children and adults.

title: About Vaccine Information Statements
text: Clinicians can offer patients the current CDC VIS as a handout. VIS documents support conversations about benefits and risks; the clinician remains responsible for individual medical advice. A VIS is not a treatment order or a personalized recommendation.

title: Current Vaccine Information Statements
text: CDC provides Vaccine Information Statements on web pages and as printable PDF documents. Some VIS files are also available as rich text for clinical electronic systems. The CDC index identifies the editions and dates of current VIS documents.

title: Current Vaccine Information Statements
text: A Vaccine Information Statement may be marked interim when its final edition is pending. Providers should consult the current CDC VIS index before giving a particular VIS because versions can be updated.

title: VIS Frequently Asked Questions
text: A Vaccine Information Statement is an education document and does not itself serve as an informed-consent form. State-specific consent rules may have additional requirements. A healthcare professional or appropriate local authority can clarify local requirements.

title: HPV Vaccine Information Statement
text: The human papillomavirus vaccine protects against infection by certain types of HPV. Some HPV infections cause cancers including cervical, anal, penile and throat cancers. HPV vaccination helps prevent many cancers caused by HPV.

title: HPV Vaccine Information Statement
text: HPV can spread through close skin-to-skin sexual contact. The vaccine is most useful before exposure to the types of HPV it targets. The CDC VIS points readers to a health professional for individualized vaccination decisions.

title: HPV Vaccine Information Statement
text: Patients should tell their vaccination provider about previous serious allergic reactions to a vaccine or its components. Any question involving a person's medical history, exact eligibility or number of doses requires a qualified clinician.

title: MMR Vaccine Information Statement
text: The MMR vaccine helps prevent three infectious diseases: measles, mumps and rubella. These illnesses can cause serious complications. MMR is different from MMRV, which also includes protection against varicella, also called chickenpox.

title: MMR Vaccine Information Statement
text: Before an MMR vaccination, patients should discuss a history of serious allergies, pregnancy, or weakened immunity with the vaccination provider. This educational chatbot cannot decide whether MMR vaccination is safe for a particular patient.

title: MMRV Vaccine Information Statement
text: The MMRV vaccine targets measles, mumps, rubella and varicella, also known as chickenpox. Unlike MMR, MMRV includes the varicella component. A clinician should select the appropriate vaccine for a specific patient.

title: Tdap Vaccine Information Statement
text: Tdap protects against tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis, also known as whooping cough. Tetanus bacteria can enter through wounds, while diphtheria and pertussis can spread between people. Specific timing and eligibility should be checked using current clinical guidance.

title: Tdap Vaccine Information Statement
text: A provider should assess previous vaccine reactions and other medical factors before vaccination. The Tdap Vaccine Information Statement describes the illnesses it targets and highlights precautions to discuss with a professional.

title: Shingles Vaccine Information Statement
text: Recombinant zoster vaccine helps prevent shingles, a painful blistering rash caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus. Preventing shingles also reduces the risk of postherpetic neuralgia, which is lasting nerve pain following the illness.

title: Shingles Vaccine Information Statement
text: Shingles can cause complications, and risk rises with age or certain immune problems. Whether an individual should receive a vaccine or follow a particular schedule needs assessment by a medical professional.

title: Possible Side Effects from Vaccines
text: Many vaccines can cause temporary effects, such as soreness at the injection site or a mild fever. Side effects vary by vaccine, and most common effects resolve within a few days. The CDC monitors vaccine safety.

title: Possible Side Effects from Vaccines
text: A severe allergic reaction following vaccination is a medical emergency. Difficulty breathing, swelling of the throat, or similar severe symptoms require emergency help. Patients with other concerning symptoms should contact a healthcare professional.

title: VIS Instructions for Providers
text: Under applicable federal requirements, vaccine providers give the current Vaccine Information Statement before administering each covered dose. The document informs recipients about vaccine benefits and risks. Recordkeeping and other requirements may apply.

title: MMR Vaccine Information Statement
text: The MMR Vaccine Information Statement explains that serious allergic reactions are rare but require urgent attention. Vaccine reactions can be reported to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, known as VAERS. Reporting is not the same as establishing that the vaccine caused the event.

title: HPV Vaccine Information Statement
text: Some types of human papillomavirus may persist and later contribute to cancer. The HPV vaccine is a prevention tool; it is not a treatment for an existing cancer or infection. A clinician can discuss appropriate screening and prevention with a patient.

title: VIS Frequently Asked Questions
text: Because a Vaccine Information Statement covers the risks and benefits of vaccination, it supports patient understanding. However, CDC explains that a VIS is not a legally interchangeable substitute for informed consent.

title: COVID-19 Vaccination Benefits — CDC
text: The COVID-19 vaccine helps protect against COVID-19, the disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Its most important benefit is reducing the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death. Vaccination cannot guarantee that a person will never get COVID-19.

title: COVID-19 Vaccination Benefits — CDC
text: People who get COVID-19 despite vaccination can have a shorter or less severe illness. Studies summarized by CDC also show that people who are vaccinated and later get infected have a lower risk of Long COVID than those who are unvaccinated or not up to date.

title: COVID-19 Vaccine Information Statement — CDC
text: COVID-19 vaccination helps the body learn to defend itself against the virus that causes COVID-19. The vaccine can help prevent COVID-19 disease and lower the severity of illness if infection occurs. It also reduces the risk of serious complications.

title: COVID-19 Vaccine Information Statement — CDC
text: After COVID-19 vaccination, possible reactions include soreness, swelling, or redness at the injection site, fatigue, headache, fever, chills, and muscle pain. Myocarditis and pericarditis have rarely been observed after COVID-19 vaccination. Anyone with concerning symptoms should contact a healthcare professional.
